- `sed` / `awk` (in-place edit) → `Edit`
- `echo > file` / `cat <<EOF` → `Write`
- `find` / recursive `ls` to locate files by name pattern → `Glob` (plain `ls <known-directory>` is fine for listing a directory)
- `grep` / `rg` (search file contents) → `Grep`
- `echo` / `printf` (talk to the user) → just output text directly

The dedicated tools render in the per-tool permission UI and keep raw stdout out of the conversation; that is why they are worth reaching for whenever one fits.

**Output:**
The stdout and stderr will be combined and returned as a string. The output may be truncated if it is too long. If the command exits non-zero, the output ends with a `Command failed with exit code: N` line; a command killed by its timeout or interrupted by the user ends with its own message instead.

Background execution is disabled for this agent. Do not set `run_in_background=true`.

**Guidelines for safety and security:**
- Each shell tool call will be executed in a fresh shell environment. The shell variables, current working directory changes, and the shell history is not preserved between calls. To run a command in a particular directory, pass the `cwd` argument (or use absolute paths) rather than relying on a `cd` from an earlier call.
- The tool call will return after the command is finished. You shall not use this tool to execute an interactive command or a command that may run forever. For possibly long-running commands, set the `timeout` argument in seconds. The default is 60s; foreground commands allow up to 300s; a foreground command that hits its timeout is killed.
- Avoid using `..` to access files or directories outside of the working directory.
- Avoid modifying files outside of the working directory unless explicitly instructed to do so.
- Never run commands that require superuser privileges unless explicitly instructed to do so.

**Guidelines for efficiency:**
- Use `&&` to chain commands that genuinely depend on each other, e.g. `npm install && npm test`. Independent read-only commands (separate `git show`, `ls`, or status checks) should be issued as separate parallel Bash calls in one response, not chained into a single call — chaining serializes their execution and mixes their output. Do not stitch outputs together with `echo` separators.

- Use `||` for conditional execution (run second command only if first fails)
- Use pipe operations (`|`) and redirections (`>`, `>>`) to chain input and output between commands
- Always quote file paths containing spaces with double quotes (e.g., cd "/path with spaces/")

tools.description:
Find files by glob pattern, sorted by modification time (most recent first).

Powered by ripgrep. Respects `.gitignore`, `.ignore`, and `.rgignore` by default — set `include_ignored` to also match ignored files (e.g. build outputs, `node_modules`). Sensitive files (such as `.env`) are always filtered out. Matches are files only — directories themselves are never listed; to find a directory, glob for a file inside it (e.g. `**/fixtures/**`).

Good patterns:
- `*.ts` — all files matching an extension, at any depth below the search root (a bare pattern without `/` matches recursively)
- `src/*.ts` — files directly inside `src/` (one level, not recursive)
- `src/**/*.ts` — recursive walk with a subdirectory anchor and extension
- `**/*.py` — recursive walk from the search root for an extension
- `*.{ts,tsx}` — brace expansion is supported

## Inferred exact algorithms (byte-wise, ASCII-only case ops throughout)

All case conversions use C `toupper`/`tolower` semantics on single bytes: only `a-z`/`A-Z` are affected; non-ASCII UTF-8 bytes, digits, `_`, spaces pass through unchanged.

- **L3 camelize(word) [default]**: Split on `'_'`. Keep segment 0 exactly as-is. For each subsequent segment, uppercase its first byte (ASCII only), keep the rest of the segment unchanged. Concatenate. Empty segments contribute nothing (`a__b`→`aB`). A leading `_` makes segment 0 empty, so the first real segment gets capitalized (`_foo`→`Foo`, `_id`→`Id`). Case of non-first bytes is preserved (`foo_bAR`→`fooBAR`, `a_bCD`→`aBCD`). Spaces/hyphens are not special.
- **L4 camelize(word,false)**: Same as L3, then uppercase byte 0 of the result (ASCII only). `cat`→`Cat`, `1abc`→`1abc`, `␣␣lead`→`␣␣lead` (leading spaces unaffected), `über`→`über`.
- **L5 underscore(word)**: For each byte at index i: if it is ASCII uppercase, emit `'_'` unless i==0, then emit the lowercased byte; otherwise emit byte as-is. No grouping of consecutive capitals: `CAT`→`c_a_t`, `ABCd`→`a_b_cd`, `A1B`→`a1_b`. Existing underscores are kept (so `Foo_Bar`→`foo__bar`). Digits/spaces untouched.
- **L8 humanize(word)**: Replace every `'_'` with `' '` (all of them, including trailing: `foo_`→`Foo␣`, `a__b`→`A␣␣b`), then uppercase byte 0 if ASCII lowercase. Does NOT strip `_id` (`post_id`→`Post id`), does NOT singularize (`post_ids`→`Post ids`, known `classes`→`Classes`), does not touch the rest of the string's case (`foo_bAR`→`Foo bAR`, `CatDog`→`CatDog`, `CAT`→`CAT`).
- **L9 titleize(word)**: Downcase the entire string (ASCII), then uppercase every ASCII-lowercase byte that is at index 0 or immediately follows a whitespace byte (space and tab confirmed — presumably `std::isspace`; `-`, `.`, `_` are NOT boundaries: `foo-bar baz.qux`→`Foo-bar Baz.qux`, `cat_dog`→`Cat_dog`). Multiple spaces: the space itself isn't a letter, the letter after the last space gets uppercased (`two␣␣spaces`→`Two␣␣Spaces`, `␣␣lead`→`␣␣Lead`).
- **L10 dasherize(word)**: Replace every `'_'` with `'-'`. Nothing else (spaces, case, digits untouched: `two␣␣spaces`→`two␣␣spaces`, `CatDog`→`CatDog`, `a__b`→`a--b`).
- **L13 upcase(word)**: ASCII `a-z`→`A-Z` on every byte; all other bytes (including UTF-8 multibyte) unchanged. `über`→`üBER`, `ß`→`ß`.
- **L14 downcase(word)**: ASCII `A-Z`→`a-z` on every byte; others unchanged. `Élan`→`Élan`.
- **L15 capitalize(word)**: Downcase the entire string (ASCII), then uppercase byte 0 if ASCII lowercase. Differs from titleize on strings with internal whitespace: `hello world`→`Hello world` vs titleize `Hello world`; `␣␣lead`→`␣␣lead` (byte 0 is a space, no-op). Identical to titleize only for single tokens without whitespace.
- **L16 decapitalize(word)**: Lowercase byte 0 if ASCII uppercase; rest of string untouched. `Foo_Bar`→`foo_Bar`, `CAT`→`cAT`, `a b c`→`␣b c`, `_`→`_`, `␣␣lead`→`␣␣lead`.

### Answers to the key questions
- (a) camelize keeps the rest of each segment's case as-is (no lowercasing); only the segment's first byte is uppercased. Leading `_` → empty first segment → first real segment is treated as a "subsequent" segment and capitalized.
- (b) underscore handles consecutive uppercase with no acronym logic: `ABCd`→`a_b_cd` (each uppercase byte except at index 0 gets its own `_`).
- (c) titleize == capitalize only when the word contains no whitespace; with spaces/tabs they differ (titleize capitalizes each whitespace-delimited word, capitalize only byte 0).
- (d) humanize does NOT strip `_id` and does NOT singularize — it's purely `_`→space + uppercase first byte.
- (e) dasherize is exactly `'_'`→`'-'`, nothing more.
- (f) upcase/downcase (and all other case ops) are byte-wise ASCII-only; UTF-8 continuation/lead bytes pass through verbatim.
- Empty input: binary aborts with `std::out_of_range` before printing anything (exit 134) — a Rust reimplementation should replicate or at least be aware of this crash-on-empty behavior.
